newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba suggests search has found Che Guevara remains.
newsitem.headline: Cuba suggests search has found Che Guevara remains.

text.p: Cuba on Thursday cautiously supported researchers' claims that they had probably found the remains of legendary Cuban revolutionary Ernesto "Che" Guevara in Bolivia.
Bolivian officials in La Paz said on Wednesday that a team searching near the town of Vallegrande in Bolivia's jungle highlands had found what were "very probably" Guevara's bones.
"We are probably very close to the result we have been seeking," said Marcos Tufino, the Bolivian official coordinating the dig at Vallegrande, 480 miles (775 km) southeast of La Paz.

Guevara, an Argentine-born doctor, was President Fidel Castro's deputy in the guerrilla struggle that led to the 1959 revolution in Cuba and became one of the island's heroes. He was captured by Bolivian troops and killed in October 1967 while leading an abortive guerrilla uprising in Bolivia.
His body was put on display as a trophy before the world press. His hands were chopped off as proof of his capture before he was buried at a secret site by his executioners.
Cuba's ruling Communist Party newspaper Granma, in a long "statement to the people" on its front page, echoed some of the research team's optimism, but with considerable caution.

Granma outlined the history of the search for Guevara's remains that began in December, 1995, and said that according to historical investigations the bodies of seven guerrillas including Guevara were dumped in a common grave near Vallegrande in the early hours of Oct. 11, 1967.

Granma described how in the last week the search team had found parts of some seven bodies near Vallegrande's old airstrip. It did not say flatly that it thought Guevara's remains were among them, but if seven bodies were found it would be most likely that one of them was his.

Bolivia began the quest for Guevara's bones after retired Gen. Mario Vargas Salinas broke two decades of silence to say he could identify the spot where he ordered the burial of the guerrillas. So far anthropologists have turned up three skeletons, at least one of which has been identified as belonging to Che Guevara's tiny revolutionary column.

Cuba has not said what it would do if Guevara's remains are found. But Cuban authorities said when the search was launched in 1995 that his family would have the right to decide the final destination of the remains.
Guevara's Cuban widow, Aleida March, still lives in Cuba.
